newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish army chief fired after row with ruling left.
newsitem.headline: Polish army chief fired after row with ruling left.

text.p: Poland's president on Monday sacked armed forces chief General Tadeusz Wilecki, whose long dispute with the ruling ex-communist party had erupted afresh just months before talks on NATO entry are due to start.

"I expect...we will be able to focus more on what needs to be done in the army and not on squabbles over personnel, rows and discussions in the mass media," President Aleksander Kwasniewski said as he appointed General Henryk Szumski, 53, to succeed Wilecki as chief of the general staff,

Critics have long accused Wilecki of trying to entrench the general staff's authority at the defence ministry's expense, harming Poland's bid to meet exacting standards for civilian control of the army required by NATO from future members.

Wilecki denies he has undermined civilian control, while arguing that he has provided vital stability of leadership and battled for adequate funds as the army prepared for NATO entry through five years of changing governments and ministers.
Wilecki said the president had succumbed to political pressure from the ex-communists.
"The president...gave in to a political grouping which has the motto: 'Those who are not with us are against us," he said at a ceremony where he handed over to Szumski.
With the Czech Republic and Hungary, Poland expects to be among the first countries invited at NATO's July summit in Madrid to start formal negotiations on joining the alliance.
Wilecki's smouldering row with Kwasniewski's allies, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), erupted again last week when a party leader said it was time to remove him.

Their dispute dates at least from late 1994 when general staff officers, at a lunch attended by then President Lech Walesa, were reported to have voted to oust the civilian defence minister of the day, Piotr Kolodziejczyk.
Walesa, who sympathised with Wilecki and the generals, sacked the minister, arousing concerns in NATO that parliamentary control of the forces was inadequate in Poland.

Poland, eager not to give Western critics of a larger NATO any pretexts to block the process, addressed the issue in a sweeping reform of command and control structures last year which entrenched the civilian defence ministry's position.
Western diplomats say that, as chief of general staff, Wilecki had tried to circumvent some of these changes.
However, rightist opposition figures backed Wilecki, saying the ex-communists were out to place their own people in key army and other posts before general elections later this year.
"They realise they will lose the polls and they want their own people in key posts of state administration," Leszek Moczulski of the Confederation for an Independent Poland told PAP news agency.

In a radio interview on Monday, Wilecki accused the SLD of reneging on promises in 1995 to spend three percent of gross domestic product on defence, saying the current 2.3 percent was inadequate to modernise and properly look after the army.

Kwasniewski told a news conference after naming Wilecki's successor that he had offered Wilecki a post in the presidential offices and a year's secondment for training in Britain, but the 52-year-old general had refused.

Defence Minister Stanislaw Dobrzanski said he had completed drafting a new law on modernisation of the forces, providing for greater spending to meet NATO requirements, and this would be studied by the cabinet defence committee on Thursday.
Wilecki has received support over the past week not only from the opposition but also from the Polish Peasant party (PSL), the SLD's smaller partner in the ruling coalition.
